headline: Hot nights cost people a week of sleep a year

sources.title: Climate change is stealing our sleep
India among global hotspots for climate-related sleep loss, highest in TN: Report
Climate Change is Costing People Sleep
New study shows more Americans are losing sleep due to the heat than ever before (video, ABC13 Houston)

chunks.text: Hot nights are costing the average person about 56 hours of sleep a year, [[close to]] seven nights' [[worth]], according to an [[analysis]] of 1,338 cities published on July 15 by the research group Climate Central. [[Roughly]] six of those hours, about one night, {{come down to}} human-caused [[warming]]. That [[share]] has [[at least]] doubled since the early 1970s, and it is far larger in some regions than others.

verbs.correct: To be explained by one main cause
verbs.wrong: To think of a new plan or idea
verbs.why: A tough decision can come down to simple cost, and a team's loss might come down to one missed shot. In this study, about six of the fifty-six lost hours come down to human-caused warming.

chunks.text: Heat {{keeps people up}} for a simple reason. Sleep [[depends on]] the body's ability to cool itself, and warm night air {{slows that cooling down}}. [[Rather than]] measure bedrooms, the team applied each city's lowest overnight temperature to a relationship between heat and sleep. An earlier study had [[established]] that relationship using data from nearly 50,000 people wearing [[sleep trackers]]. Kelton Minor of the University of Copenhagen, who led that study, said, "The warmer it gets, the less that people sleep."

verbs.why: Loud neighbors can keep you up half the night, and a strong coffee in the evening might keep you up for hours. Warm night air keeps people up because it slows the body's natural cooling.

verbs.correct: To make something happen more slowly
verbs.wrong: To stop a machine from working
verbs.why: Traffic can slow down your whole morning commute, and a slow internet connection can slow down a video call. Warm night air slows the body's natural cooling down, making it harder for people to fall asleep.

chunks.text: People in parts of southern India and Southeast Asia lose 78 to 91 hours a year to warm nights, [[against]] 36 hours across 253 US cities. Chennai loses more than any other Indian city, 93 hours. The team was [[open about]] one [[weakness]]: the sleep research behind its [[model]] was based mostly on people in higher-[[income]] countries, where [[cooling]] is easier to {{come by}}, so losses in poorer places may be bigger than these [[figures]] [[suggest]].

verbs.wrong: To become known to the public
verbs.why: Good jobs can be hard to come by in a small town, and fresh fish is easy to come by near the coast. In wealthier countries, cooling like air conditioning is much easier to come by than in poorer ones.

chunks.text: The effect of warm nights was [[twice as large]] for adults over 65 and three times as large for people on lower-middle incomes. About 35 percent of [[households]] worldwide owned an [[air conditioner]] in 2021, and ownership [[tracks]] income closely. A few lost minutes are easy to {{shrug off}}. Over a year they {{add up}} to a week.

verbs.wrong: To raise your shoulders to show doubt
verbs.why: An athlete might shrug off a small injury before a big game, and a driver can shrug off a minor delay in traffic. A few minutes of lost sleep each night are easy to shrug off, though they matter over time.

verbs.correct: To grow gradually into a larger total
verbs.wrong: To attach an extra part to something
verbs.why: Small tips can add up over a busy week of work, and daily savings can add up to a large amount over a year. A few lost minutes each night seem small, but over a year they add up to a full week of sleep.

mainIdea.s: A new study finds that warmer nights take about a week of sleep from most people each year. Older adults and lower income households lose even more, since they often cannot afford cooling.
mainIdea.why: The analysis found about 56 hours of lost sleep a year from heat. That effect is twice as large for adults over 65 and three times as large for lower income people.

mainIdea.s: The study says human-caused warming is now behind nearly all the average person's lost sleep each year. It also found that the effect is the same for every age group and income level.
mainIdea.why: Close, but only about six of the 56 lost hours are tied to human-caused warming. The effect is also far larger for older adults and lower income people, not equal across groups.

mainIdea.s: A separate report this summer counted a rise in heat-related hospital visits in southern Asia. Officials there opened cooling centers to protect elderly residents during the hottest months.
mainIdea.why: This story is about a rise in heat-related hospital visits and new cooling centers in southern Asia, not sleep loss from warm nights.
